name: The Vagrant Ember

stars.name: The Vagrant
stars.notes: Methane brown dwarf, surface temperature approximately 1,100 K; technically a failed star, emitting only dim infrared light

planets.name: Orphan
planets.notes: Rogue gas giant gravitationally captured by the brown dwarf roughly 2 billion years ago. Mass rivals its host, making the pair nearly a binary system of failed stars.

anomalies.name: Inverted Mass Ratio
anomalies.location: Barycenter between The Vagrant and Orphan
anomalies.notes: The gas giant is nearly 80% the mass of its host star. The pair orbit a shared barycenter located in open space between them, creating a slow, wobbling dance visible in infrared.

anomalies.name: Methane Aurora Cascade
anomalies.notes: Interaction between the brown dwarf's weak magnetic field and Orphan's own magnetosphere produces faint methane aurorae visible to tuned sensors—shifting curtains of deep red and violet.

anomalies.name: The Cold Lagrange
anomalies.location: L4 and L5 points between The Vagrant and Orphan
anomalies.notes: Captured interstellar debris has accumulated at the Lagrange points over billions of years, forming two faint clouds of ice and rock that predate both bodies' partnership.

faction_control.notes: No faction has claimed this system. It lies far from trade routes and offers nothing of conventional value.

history: Discovered in 2487 by a long-range infrared survey satellite, initially cataloged as an isolated brown dwarf with an unusually large companion.
A 2511 expedition confirmed Orphan as a captured rogue gas giant, making this one of the few known examples of a brown dwarf with a planetary-mass companion acquired through gravitational capture.
No crewed vessel has visited the system since the initial survey. Automated probes continue to relay data on the methane aurorae and Lagrange debris clouds.
description: The Vagrant Ember is a system in name only—a dim methane brown dwarf and its improbable companion, a rogue gas giant snared from the interstellar void billions of years ago. The Vagrant itself radiates so little visible light that the pair would be invisible to the naked eye at even modest astronomical distances. In infrared, however, they form a striking binary: two bloated spheres of gas, one barely a star, the other not even that, locked in a slow gravitational waltz around a shared center of mass.

What makes the system singular is the near-parity of its components. Orphan masses roughly 80% of its host, an almost unheard-of ratio that blurs the line between star-and-planet and binary-failed-star. Their shared Lagrange points have accumulated billions of years of interstellar flotsam—ice grains, carbon dust, primordial pebbles older than either body. The methane aurorae that flicker across The Vagrant's upper atmosphere are the only color in an otherwise lightless void, produced by the gentle collision of two weak magnetospheres.

There is no strategic reason to come here. No resources worth extracting, no habitable real estate, no navigational significance. The Vagrant Ember exists as a curiosity—a cosmic odd couple drifting through the outer dark, proof that gravity will find companionship even in the emptiest reaches of space. Researchers have proposed the pair as a natural laboratory for studying brown dwarf magnetospheres and captured-body orbital mechanics, but funding has never materialized. For now, the two drift on, unvisited and unbothered.
